reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / endocrine and neuromuscular reference literature
clinicalPearls: Presents with acute episodes of proximal, often ascending, muscle weakness or flaccid paralysis in the setting of thyrotoxicosis and profound hypokalaemia
Characteristically affects young Asian men, most often on a background of Graves disease, although any cause of thyrotoxicosis can be responsible
Attacks are commonly triggered by a high-carbohydrate meal, strenuous exercise followed by rest, or stress, typically overnight or in the early morning
The hypokalaemia reflects an intracellular shift of potassium rather than true depletion, driven by thyroid-hormone-enhanced sodium-potassium-ATPase activity
Thyrotoxic symptoms may be subtle, so thyroid function should be checked in any young man with hypokalaemic paralysis
Acute treatment uses cautious potassium and beta-blockade for thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, with close monitoring to avoid rebound hyperkalaemia
Definitive prevention depends on rendering the patient euthyroid, after which attacks cease
reference.pathophysiology: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis arises when excess thyroid hormone increases the activity of the sodium-potassium-ATPase pump in skeletal muscle, driving potassium into cells. This intracellular shift is amplified by insulin and adrenergic stimulation, explaining the triggering by carbohydrate loads, exercise and stress. The resulting acute hypokalaemia hyperpolarises and then paradoxically renders muscle membranes inexcitable, producing flaccid weakness. Because potassium is redistributed rather than lost, total body potassium is normal, which underlies the risk of rebound hyperkalaemia if too much potassium is administered. A genetic predisposition affecting muscle ion channels is thought to contribute in susceptible individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Hypokalaemia from gastrointestinal or renal potassium loss
Renal tubular acidosis or Gitelman/Bartter syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium and full electrolyte panel during the attack
Electrocardiogram to detect hypokalaemic changes and arrhythmia
Assessment of urinary potassium and acid-base status to confirm a shift rather than loss
TSH-receptor antibodies and thyroid imaging to define the cause of thyrotoxicosis
redFlags: Respiratory muscle involvement or bulbar weakness compromising ventilation
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent once euthyroidism is achieved, as attacks resolve completely; recurrence is the rule while thyrotoxicosis persists.
pitfalls: Overzealous potassium replacement causing dangerous rebound hyperkalaemia as potassium redistributes
Missing subtle thyrotoxicosis in a young man presenting with paralysis
Confusing the condition with familial periodic paralysis and overlooking the thyroid cause
Failing to treat the underlying thyrotoxicosis, leaving the patient prone to further attacks
Neglecting cardiac monitoring during acute hypokalaemia
references: Reference literature on thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
